author: AI Editorial Team (Esi)
key_learning_objective: Interpret an elevated BNP in the context of heart failure.
question_stem: A client is admitted with dyspnea. The B-type natriuretic peptide (BNP) is 1,200 pg/mL. The nurse interprets this result as:

options.A: Within normal limits, ruling out a cardiac cause
options.B: Consistent with fluid overload from heart failure
options.C: An indication of acute myocardial infarction

rationales.A: Normal BNP is generally < 100 pg/mL; 1,200 pg/mL is markedly elevated.
rationales.B: Correct. BNP is released when ventricles are stretched by volume/pressure overload; a high value supports heart failure with fluid overload as the cause of the dyspnea.
rationales.C: Troponin, not BNP, is the marker for myocardial injury/MI.
rationales.D: Dehydration reduces ventricular stretch and would not elevate BNP.

key_takeaway: BNP rises with ventricular stretch. High BNP + dyspnea points to heart failure, not MI (that's troponin).
nclex_test_taking_tip: Anchor each cardiac lab to its meaning: BNP = stretch/volume, troponin = muscle injury.
memory_trick: BNP = Big Nasty Pressure on the ventricle.
clinical_pearls: BNP helps distinguish cardiac from pulmonary causes of dyspnea.
Trending BNP can track response to diuresis.
